notes.b: Dietary guidelines are official advice, based on scientific evidence, on the types and amounts of food that keep a population healthy. They turn nutrition science into practical advice for the general healthy population, and are revised as evidence changes.
points: Evidence comes from nutrition research, national food consumption surveys (which record what people actually eat) and health data on diet-related diseases.

Expert committees review this evidence and turn it into practical advice on foods rather than nutrients, setting the types of food to eat and the amounts to limit. The guidelines are reviewed as new evidence appears.

The Department of Health publishes the healthy eating guidelines for Ireland and the Food Pyramid, which is one of the tools used to explain them (the current pyramid is called 'Healthy Food for Life', 2016).
The HSE supports the guidelines, and the Food Safety Authority of Ireland (FSAI) and safefood are other Irish bodies in this field.
The guidelines are written for the general healthy population, so they are not a substitute for advice for individuals with special medical needs.

The aims are to make sure people get enough nutrients, to prevent deficiency, and to reduce the risk of obesity, type 2 diabetes, coronary heart disease, high blood pressure, stroke, some cancers and osteoporosis (weak, brittle bones).
One consistent message also helps consumers, schools and food planners, because everyone is working from the same advice.
notes.tip: The Food Pyramid is not the same thing as the guidelines. The guidelines are the advice, and the pyramid is the picture and servings that put them into practice.

notes.h: Principles of the healthy eating guidelines
notes.b: The Irish guidelines can be given as about eight principles. Together they say which foods to eat most, which to eat in moderation and which to keep small.
points: Eat plenty of vegetables, salad and fruit: about five to seven portions a day, spread across meals.
Base meals on starchy foods, choosing wholegrain bread, cereals, potatoes, pasta and rice.
Include protein from lean meat, poultry, fish, eggs, beans, lentils and nuts, with fish eaten regularly.
Choose milk, yoghurt and cheese in lower-fat forms, as they supply calcium and HBV protein (high biological value protein, which contains all the essential amino acids).
Use fats and oils sparingly, and prefer unsaturated oils such as rapeseed and olive oil.
Limit foods and drinks high in fat, sugar and salt, which are not needed for health and should be occasional.
Drink water as the main drink, and keep alcohol within recommended limits.
Eat regular meals and prepare food with methods that add little fat, such as steaming, grilling and baking.
notes.tip: Healthy eating guidelines are the basis for menu planning in nearly every menu question. When you write three meals, follow the guidelines and justify each choice.

notes.b: Each guideline is linked to a health benefit or a health risk. Examiners want the guideline and its reason together.
points: Fruit and vegetables supply fibre, vitamins, minerals and antioxidants (substances that protect cells from damage), which protect against chronic disease.
Wholegrain starchy foods give more fibre and nutrients than refined white flour products, and promote bowel health because fibre helps prevent constipation and bowel disorders.
Saturated fat raises blood cholesterol, which increases the risk of coronary heart disease.
Excess salt is linked to high blood pressure, which increases the risk of stroke and heart disease.
Sugar adds energy without nutrients, contributes to obesity, and causes tooth decay.
notes.tip: Link each guideline to a health benefit: name the food or nutrient, then the effect on the body.

notes.b: An RDA (Recommended Dietary Allowance) is a planning value: the amount of a nutrient that meets the needs of nearly all healthy people in a group.
points: An RDA is set for each nutrient and differs by age, sex and life stage, such as growth, pregnancy, lactation (breastfeeding) or adolescence.

RDAs are used to plan menus and to check that a diet supplies enough of each nutrient over the day, by comparing the day's nutrient total with the RDA. They also guide food-labelling and supplement standards and institutions such as schools and hospitals.
An RDA is a guide for a group; it is not a precise target for an individual.
Intake far above the RDA does not give extra benefit and can be harmful for some nutrients, so supplements should be used with care.
Nutrients that are often low in Irish diets, such as iron and calcium, are the ones to check against the RDA when planning a menu.
notes.tip: If asked about RDAs, define it, say what it varies with (age, sex and life stage), and say how it is used to check a menu. Don't confuse an RDA with what someone actually eats, or with the reference intake on a food label.

notes.b: A food composition table is a reference book of food values. It lets you turn a menu into numbers, so you can check it against the RDAs and the guidelines.
points: A food composition table gives the nutrient and energy content of a food, usually per 100 g of edible food. Irish tables are produced from national food analysis.
Tables state whether values are for raw or cooked food, so the matching version must be used because cooking changes the nutrient content.
Method: for each food, work out the grams eaten, divide by 100, then multiply by the value per 100 g.
Example (sample data): 150 g of a food with 3 g fibre per 100 g supplies 150 / 100 x 3 = 4.5 g fibre.
Add the results for all foods in the menu to give the day's total for each nutrient and for energy, then compare the total with the RDA. Where a total is low or high, adjust the menu.
notes.tip: Table values are per 100 g, not per portion, and raw and cooked foods are listed separately. Exams ask you to calculate nutrients in a menu, interpret a table, or explain how tables are used when planning menus.

notes.b: A computer nutrition program does the same job as a food composition table, but automatically. It is quick to use, though it is only as good as the information put in.
points: Nutrition programs contain a built-in food composition database; the user enters each food and the quantity eaten.
The program totals the energy and nutrients for the day and compares them with the guidelines or RDAs.
Check that the portion size entered matches the food as eaten, and that the correct cooking method is selected, because the results depend on correct portions and the right cooking state.
A program shows which nutrients are low or high, which helps the planner adjust the menu.
Advantages are that it is fast and accurate and holds many foods and recipes.

notes.b: The Food Pyramid turns the healthy eating guidelines into the types and relative amounts of food needed each day. Foods with similar nutrients are grouped on shelves, with the base shelf eaten most and the top shelf least.
points: The current Irish pyramid has six shelves. At the base are vegetables, salad and fruit, with wholemeal cereals and breads, potatoes, pasta and rice above them.
Next come milk, yogurt and cheese, then meat, poultry, fish, eggs, beans and nuts (including lean choices), then a small shelf of fats, spreads and oils, to be used sparingly.
The top shelf holds foods and drinks high in fat, sugar and salt. These are not needed for health, have no recommended servings, and should be occasional. Water is the main drink.

Servings: five to seven servings of vegetables, salad and fruit a day, three servings of milk, yogurt and cheese (five for ages 9 to 18), and three to five servings of wholemeal cereals, breads, potatoes, pasta and rice.

The number and size of servings from the other shelves are adjusted for age, sex, health, activity level and life stage, for example children, teenagers, pregnant and breastfeeding women and older adults.

To plan meals, take most foods from the large lower shelves, some from the middle and very little from the top, and vary the foods within each shelf. Include vegetables or fruit at every meal, and choose wholemeal and lower-fat versions.
Spread the choices across breakfast, lunch, dinner and snacks so the day covers every shelf and matches the person's portions. This supports energy balance and prevents both deficiency and excess.
The pyramid guides what to eat and roughly how much, not an exact diet, and it does not replace advice for medical conditions.
Diagram: draw the Food Pyramid, label each shelf with the main foods on it, and mark the base shelf and the top shelf.
notes.tip: Fruit and vegetables form the base shelf, with the cereals and potatoes shelf above it, so don't describe wholegrain starches as the biggest shelf. When asked how the pyramid is used to plan meals, name each shelf and its foods, say most from the base and little from the top, and add portions adjusted to age, sex and activity, variety, and the link to energy balance and disease prevention.

notes.b: A serving (portion) is a standard measure of food used to plan and count intake against the pyramid. It makes diets easy to compare, because everyone counts in the same units.
points: A portion is a standard amount of food used for planning, counting and comparing diets.
One piece of fruit, such as an apple, or one serving of vegetables counts as one portion of fruit or vegetables.
One glass of milk counts as one portion of milk, yoghurt or cheese in the dairy group.
Portion size should be adjusted to the person's age and activity: teenagers and active adults need larger portions from the starchy foods shelf than older, less active adults.
Serving sizes and numbers rise for growing teenagers and active people and fall for older, less active adults. Pregnant and breastfeeding women need extra servings of some groups.

notes.b: Food supplements are concentrates of important nutrients. They can fill a gap in a diet, but they cannot do everything that food does.
points: Food supplements are concentrates of nutrients such as vitamins, minerals, omega-3 fatty acids (polyunsaturated fatty acids) and amino acids, sold in tablet, capsule or powder form.
They may be used to fill gaps where diet is restricted, where allergies or intolerances exclude foods, or where a person has special needs.
Folic acid prevents neural tube defects (defects of the baby's brain and spine) in a developing baby when taken before conception and in early pregnancy.
Iron supplements can treat anaemia caused by low iron intake, under medical advice.
Older people may absorb nutrients less efficiently, so they may need supplements, particularly vitamin D.

Their popularity is growing for reasons such as busy lifestyles, poor diets, media and advertising, a wish to prevent illness, special needs (vegans, restricted diets, illness), sports performance and convenience.
Supplements cannot replace a varied diet, because food supplies fibre and other nutrients that supplements do not contain.

High doses of some vitamins and minerals can be harmful, especially fat-soluble vitamins, so supplements should not be taken above the recommended levels. They can also cost a lot, so take medical advice.
notes.tip: If asked to comment on the growing popularity of supplements, give a definition, a reason and a caution. Supplements are not the same as fortified foods.

notes.b: Healthy eating is only part of staying healthy. The lifestyle guidelines cover activity, mental wellbeing and habits that harm the body.
points: Regular physical activity: build activity into daily life, such as brisk walking, cycling, sport or active housework, and include muscle-strengthening and weight-bearing exercise (which loads the bones, such as walking or running).

Physical activity improves cardiovascular fitness, maintains muscle and bone, supports weight control and mental wellbeing, and may raise protective HDL cholesterol (the protective form of cholesterol).
Mental health: get adequate sleep and rest, keep a realistic workload, and use stress management, relaxation and social contact.
Avoid tobacco and second-hand smoke, which damage the lungs and blood vessels and greatly raise the risk of cancer and coronary heart disease.
Limit alcohol: it supplies empty kilocalories (energy with no nutrients), harms the liver and judgement, and must never be used to manage stress.
Drink plenty of water and keep a healthy body weight.
Regular health checks and good personal hygiene complete the guidelines.
Together these habits reduce the risk of obesity, type 2 diabetes, hypertension (high blood pressure) and heart disease.
notes.tip: When asked to describe three lifestyle guidelines, choose from activity, sleep and stress management, and avoiding tobacco and limiting alcohol, and give a benefit for each.

keyTerms.definition: Official advice on the types and amounts of food needed to maintain health and prevent disease.
The intake of a nutrient that meets the needs of nearly all healthy people in a group, used as a planning guide.
A table of the nutrient and energy content of foods, usually per 100 g of edible food.
A diagram of stacked shelves showing the foods to eat most often at the base and those to use sparingly at the top.
A standard amount of a food group used for planning and counting servings in a diet.
A concentrated source of a nutrient in tablet, capsule or powder form, taken in addition to food.
A fat, mainly from animal foods, that raises blood cholesterol when eaten in excess.
Indigestible plant material in wholegrain foods, fruit and vegetables that aids bowel function.

questions.prompt: Outline two ways a food composition table is used when planning a menu.
questions.model: The table gives the nutrient and energy content per 100 g of food, so the amount eaten can be calculated by scaling the value to the portion. The totals for all foods in a day's menu can then be compared with the RDA for each nutrient, showing which nutrients are low or high and where the menu needs adjusting. Full marks require the link between the table values and the calculation or comparison.

questions.prompt: Explain how the Food Pyramid is used to plan healthy balanced meals, and describe three lifestyle guidelines that support good health.
questions.model: Food Pyramid: it converts guidelines into types and relative amounts of food; the larger lower shelves are chosen most often and the small top shelf is used sparingly. Fruit and vegetables, about five to seven portions a day, appear at every meal for fibre, vitamins and minerals. Wholegrain cereals, bread, potatoes, pasta and rice provide the main carbohydrate. Dairy and protein foods are chosen in lower-fat forms and lean choices; fish is included regularly. Fats, sugar and salt are limited, water is the main drink, and portions are adjusted for age, sex, health and activity to achieve energy balance. Lifestyle: regular physical activity; sleep, rest and stress management; avoiding tobacco and limiting alcohol. These reduce the risk of obesity, type 2 diabetes, hypertension and heart disease.
